kurz: Why every purchase has three prices, only the first of which is on the label, and what this means for cars, subscriptions and pay rises.

bloecke.md:
Every purchase has three prices. The first is the purchase price on the label. The second is incurred continuously for as long as the thing exists, for example for insurance, electricity, maintenance, fees and parking. The third, which is never stated anywhere, is the return that the tied-up money would have earned over the same period if it had been used differently. A comparison that considers only the first price therefore rests on a third of the information.

Distinguishing between the three prices has nothing to do with morality. A car that costs three hundred euros a month in depreciation is justifiable if it is worth three hundred euros a month to its owner. It only becomes a mistake if nobody ever worked out that it is three hundred euros a month.

bloecke.formel: True cost = (Purchase price − Residual value) + running costs + return on tied-up capital
bloecke.erklaerung: The first term is depreciation, and for durable goods it is almost always the largest. The third does not appear on any statement when you pay cash, because it is never debited. Money that is tied up in a car cannot be invested in a portfolio at the same time.
variablen: acquisition price including delivery, registration and accessories
realistically achievable sale price at the end of the useful life
everything that is incurred every year without you deciding on it again
the value still contained in the item at any given time, not the original purchase price

bloecke.md:
## Lifestyle inflation

The term [[lifestyle inflation]] is used when spending rises with income rather than with prices. This is due to a property of fixed costs, not to character. The decision for a bigger flat, a lease or a second subscription is made once and then paid for two hundred and forty times. After three months, the pay rise no longer feels like additional money, but the standing order remains.

A worked example with two households shows the order of magnitude. Both start with €2,800 net and €2,400 in spending, both initially save €400 a month, and both receive the same income increases of 3.5% a year. The first household raises its spending only in line with rising prices, assumed here at 2.5%. In the second, spending rises at the same rate as income. The savings go into a portfolio assumed to return 6% a year. That is slightly less than the 7.7% that the MSCI World achieved net in euros from 1970 to 2025.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio value of two households with the same income over twenty years (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: Both households start with the same monthly savings amount of €400 and invest in the same way. The difference arises solely from whether the annual increase goes into savings or into spending.

bloecke.md:
After twenty years, the first household has €354,800 in its portfolio, the second €240,100. The difference of around €115,000 is not due to better investing. Both invest in the same way, only with different savings amounts. In the first household, the [[savings rate]] has grown from 14% to 29%; in the second, it remains unchanged at 14%.

The second household has not lost the money. In the final year it spends €4,614 instead of €3,837 a month and therefore lives €777 a month better. Whether that was worth the €115,000 cannot be calculated. It only becomes a mistake if this question was never asked and the increases flowed into fixed costs that nobody remembers taking on.

A pay rise is only easy to save before it is paid out for the first time. If the savings plan is increased by half of the net increase in the same month, there is no sense of going without. Your standard of living still rises, just more slowly than your income.

## The cost of a car

With cars, people are particularly unlikely to do the maths, even though depreciation in the first years is almost always greater than interest, energy and repairs combined. It hardly gets noticed because no bill arrives for it. It only becomes apparent when the car is sold.

The following calculation assumes a new car costing €36,000 and declining-balance depreciation of 16% a year. On this basis, the car is worth €17,900 after four years and €8,900 after eight years. This is a model assumption, not a market value. Depending on the make, drive type and demand, the curve is considerably flatter or steeper. Running costs are left out because they are similar in all four variants. The alternative return on your own capital is set at a cautious 4%, because four years is a short horizon for equities. The loan interest rate of 6.2% is the median for instalment loans taken out via a comparison website in August 2026. It is a figure from that website, not a market average.

bloecke.titel: Four ways of using a car over four years, depreciation and capital costs only (illustrative calculation)
Cost components over four years (in euros)
bloecke.unter: Depreciation varies more between the variants than interest does. Depreciation depends on the vehicle, not on the method of payment.

bloecke.md:
The table leads to three observations. First, at around €1,600 over four years, the gap between paying cash and financing is the smallest difference between any two variants. With a loan, too, your own money gradually flows into the car through the repayments, and it then earns no return. The gap reverses as soon as the loan interest rate falls below the alternative return. Second, leasing costs more than buying here. The leasing company passes on the same depreciation and adds its refinancing costs and its margin. In return, with mileage-based leasing (Kilometerleasing), it bears the risk that the [[residual value]] turns out lower at the end than calculated. The instalment of €536 that results from this breakdown corresponds to a lease rate factor of around 1.5. This factor is the instalment divided by the list price, times one hundred. Many offers are below this because manufacturers subsidise leasing to steer sales. Someone else then bears part of the cost. Just as many offers are above it.

Third, only the choice of vehicle has a large effect on the costs. In the four-year-old car, the same mobility costs €231 instead of €465 a month. The choice of car accounts for around eleven thousand euros, the choice of payment method for €1,600 to €3,400.

bloecke.titel: Smaller instalments without a cost advantage
bloecke.md:
- With **balloon or final-instalment financing**, the monthly instalment falls because a large part of the purchase price is pushed to the end. A five-figure payment then falls due, which usually has to be refinanced, often on worse terms than the original loan.
- With **residual value leasing** (Restwertleasing), unlike mileage-based leasing, the lessee is liable for the difference if the car is worth less than calculated when it is returned. An optimistically set residual value makes the instalment small and the final bill large.
- Loss of value due to damage and excess mileage is assessed from a catalogue on return, not negotiated.
- Financing without existing capital is not optimisation. If someone can only drive the car because they finance it, the instalment is no use as a benchmark for comparison. It then indicates a budget limit that has already been exceeded.

Interest-free financing is only free of charge if the dealer would not have given a discount for immediate payment. In the following example, the list price is €30,000, paid in 36 equal instalments of €833.33. Paying cash would have secured an 8% discount, so the price would have been €27,600. In effect, you borrow €27,600 and repay €30,000. The [[effective interest rate]] of this hidden loan is around 5.6% a year.

For the same term, the discount given up results in the following effective interest rates:

- with a 3% discount, around 2.0%
- with a 5% discount, around 3.4%
- with an 8% discount, around 5.6%
- with a 10% discount, around 7.2%

You should therefore ask the seller for the price if you pay immediately by bank transfer, not for the cost of financing. The difference between the two prices gives the interest rate against which to compare your own alternative return.

## The capital price of subscriptions

A standing order is more than a single expense; it is a liability with no end date. To gauge what a monthly amount means over the long term, it can be converted into the capital that would be needed to pay it permanently out of investment income.

bloecke.formel: Capital price = Monthly amount × 12 / Withdrawal rate
bloecke.erklaerung: At a withdrawal rate of 4%, every euro of permanent monthly costs corresponds to around €300 of capital. The 4% comes from a 1994 analysis of US capital market history. As a withdrawal rule it is disputed, but as a yardstick for converting permanent costs it is still useful.

bloecke.titel: Eight ongoing contracts of an example household

bloecke.md: €125.75 a month is €1,509 a year. Suppose half of this is cut because four of the eight contracts are hardly used, and the roughly €63 freed up is invested at 6% for twenty years. The result is around €28,500. The full amount would come to around €57,000. The effect of these contracts rests on the fact that none of them feels like a decision about wealth when it is taken out.

## Limits of the third price

Converting consumption into portfolio values is a strong argument, but it can also mislead. It shows what a difference long periods make. €1,000 that is not spent today becomes €5,743 in nominal terms after thirty years at 6%. However, this figure is almost always overstated. From the gain, [[flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] and the solidarity surcharge are deducted as soon as the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) has been used up. For an equity ETF this is 18.46% of the gain, because 30% remains tax-free as a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung); for individual shares it is 26.375%. The remaining amount loses a considerable part of its purchasing power to inflation. In September 2026, the inflation rate was 3.3% compared with the same month a year earlier.

bloecke.titel: Growth of €1,000 not spent (illustrative calculation, equity ETF, 6% nominal)
bloecke.unter: The opportunity cost of consumption exists, but it is smaller than the nominal figure. After tax and inflation, the factor of 5.7 over thirty years becomes a factor of just over 1.8.

bloecke.md:
In real terms and after tax, €1,000 becomes around €1,840 in today's purchasing power after thirty years. That is still an increase of just over 80%, but considerably less than the factor of 5.7 that is often cited in this argument. With an honest calculation, the argument therefore remains valid; only the exaggeration disappears.

The second limit is a logical one. Followed through consistently, calculating with [[opportunity cost]] would argue against all consumption, because every euro could be invested. But a portfolio that is never spent remains a number without any use. The useful question is therefore whether an expense offers good value and whether the decision was made deliberately at some point or came about unnoticed.

bloecke.unter: For total costs, how often an expense recurs matters more than its amount. A small monthly item costs more over the years than a large one-off.

felder.text: Inconspicuous individually, a noticeable item in the monthly budget in total. Review once a year and cancel without replacement.
This is where the savings rate is decided. The decision is made every few years and takes effect every month.

felder.titel: Coffee, a book, dinner with friends
felder.text: Optimising hardly pays here: a lot of attention, little effect, a strong sense of going without.
Rare, plannable, negotiable. Research pays off, and a mistake can be put right.

bloecke.titel: Four rules that involve no sacrifice
bloecke.md:
1. Check the recurrence first, then the amount. A one-off bad purchase of €300 costs €300; a monthly one of €30 corresponds to €9,000 of capital.
2. Work out the cost per use. €1,200 for a bike ridden twice a week comes to around €3.85 per ride over three years. The same €1,200 for a device used three times is €400 per use.
3. For larger purchases, let a night pass and write down beforehand the price you would be willing to pay. Your own figure is then the benchmark for negotiating, not the seller's price.
4. Once a year, go through your account statement looking for recurring transactions rather than amounts. Anything debited twelve times belongs on a list; one-off debits usually do not.

Averaged across all households in Germany, consumer debt in 2023 was around €2,200 and mortgage debt around €30,800. This average says little about the individual household. Consumer loans are very unequally distributed, and in the households that have such loans, they are well above this figure.

mitnehmen: The largest cost item for durable purchases is depreciation, not interest, so the choice of item carries more weight than the choice of financing.
A pay rise that is not split on the day it takes effect flows into fixed costs and can then only be recovered with noticeable sacrifice.
Monthly amounts have a capital price; at a 4% withdrawal rate, every euro of recurring costs corresponds to around €300 of wealth.
Financing at 0% costs as much as the cash discount you give up for it.
Opportunity cost should be calculated in real terms and after tax; the argument then remains valid and the figure becomes smaller.

begriffe.text: Rise in spending in line with income rather than prices. The savings rate stays constant even though the financial headroom has grown. The effect only becomes visible over years.
The forgone return of the best use that was not chosen. For consumption, this is the return that the tied-up money would have earned in a portfolio or in an instant-access savings account.

The value that can realistically be achieved at the end of the useful life. With residual value leasing, the lessee is liable for the difference from the calculated value; with mileage-based leasing, the lessor is.
Monthly instalment divided by list price, times one hundred. It makes offers roughly comparable but says nothing about the term, mileage or down payment.
The discount a dealer grants for immediate payment. If it is given up for 0% financing, the forgone discount is the interest on that financing.
